newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ABN TO END OVERLAP WITH SALE OF MEESPIERSON.
newsitem.headline: ABN TO END OVERLAP WITH SALE OF MEESPIERSON.

text.p: Banking analysts on Wednesday applauded Dutch bank ABN AMRO NV's decision to consider selling its wholly-owned MeesPierson NV investment banking unit because it would finally end a glaring overlap in their activities.
After denying rumours of the sale for several years, ABN AMRO on Tuesday said it was in talks after being approached by a number of parties interested in buying MeesPierson.
In recent years MeesPierson's retail operations, including leasing and mortgages, have been incorporated into ABN AMRO but the parent bank has also expanded into investment banking.
"It makes sense. Within ABN, MeesPierson is something of a duplication. They're often competitors," said ING Barings analyst Daan Worm.
Analysts estimate MeesPierson, which has 4,000 staff around the world, including 2,500 in the Netherlands, could fetch up to 2.5 billion guilders ($1.46 billion).
It has equity of 1.75 billion guilders and total assets of 38.6 billion guilders.
Rumours of the sale have been circulating since 1992 when the Dutch bank bought British securities house Hoare Govett in 1992 and began a path of expansion in investment banking.
MeesPierson is involved in corporate finance, specialised finance, private banking, asset management, custody and institutional services.
ABN AMRO has not revealed who it is negotiating with but analysts believe it is down to one final party.
They see Dutch-Belgian financial services group Fortis as the most likely buyer, but Dutch insurer Aegon was also touted as a prospect.
Worm said ABN AMRO had found it difficult to explain why it retained MeesPierson when it was expanding through Hoare Govett.
He expected the deal to be concluded within a few weeks. "You don't admit you want to sell if you don't have serious discussions," Worm said.
He said it could use the funds freed up from the sale to continue making small- to medium-sized acquisitions, adding that it might look to expand its loan book in South East Asia.
Ton Gietman of Van Meer James Capel said MeesPierson had actually been on the market for two or three years, although this had been officially denied by the parent bank.
"It's doing exactly the same as ABN AMRO but on a smaller scale," he said.
Generale Bank analyst Harry Luchtenveld said ABN AMRO would have no problem raising 2.0-2.5 billion guilders from the sale, adding it would be a positive move.
"The services of MeesPierson overlap considerably with ABN. They can sell it to someone more desperate for its activities," he said.
He nominated Fortis as a likely buyer, saying it wanted to add corporate banking to its retail banking activities.
Dennis Ederzeel of Delta Lloyd Bank saw the possible disposal as a good move as ABN AMRO had already stripped the "nice parts" from MeesPierson.
"What they could use, they took," he said.
He estimated a sale price of up to 2.5 billion guilders, based on net assets and a multiple of earnings.
MeesPierson's net profit rose to 132 million guilders in the first half of 1996 from 79 million a year earlier.

It was formed through a 1993 merger of Mees & Hope and Pierson Heldring & Pierson, the Dutch investment banking units of Algemene Bank Nederland (ABN) and Amsterdam-Rotterdam Bank (AMRO) which themselves merged in 1991 to form ABN AMRO. $=Dfl1.71
